documents: Gilbert et al. (2022) JGR Atmospheres 127, e2021JD034766, published paper (PDF, 17 pages)
pages_convention: PDF pages counted from 1 (identical to the printed 'n of 17' pages); supplementary material cited by section/table label because the supplement was not supplied

entry.evidence: highlights the need for a comprehensive and long-term (multidecadal) model data set

steps.action: Authors state the gap: no comprehensive multidecadal estimate of foehn frequency and its impacts on the SEB and melt over Larsen C. The only model that captured foehn-driven melt covered 6 months.
steps.quote: highlights the need for a comprehensive and long-term (multidecadal) model data set

steps.action: Authors take from the literature that hydrostatic or coarse regional climate models (MAR, RACMO) fail to reproduce the foehn-driven east-west melt gradient.
steps.quote: many struggle to reproduce the east-west gradient in melt associated with foehn winds

steps.action: Authors assemble validation data from others: AWS 14, 15, 17 and 18 records (2009-2017), with temperature and tilt corrections and SEB and melt-energy definitions, plus ERA5 reanalysis.
steps.quote: We use available AWS data from four stations, AWS 14, 15, 17, and 18

steps.action: Authors configure a nonhydrostatic MetUM (ENDGAME core, RA1M with modified cloud scheme) limited-area domain at 4 km, nested in the global model, with updated orography and land-sea mask.
steps.quote: uses a rotated latitude-longitude grid to maintain a uniform horizontal resolution of 4.0 km

steps.action: Authors rest the choice of configuration and of the 4 km resolution on their own earlier work (Gilbert et al. 2020; Gilbert 2020 thesis).
steps.quote: Gilbert et al. (2020) showed that this was the most suitable model configuration currently available for this region.

steps.action: Authors design the runs: a 1998-2017 hindcast plus a Sept 2001-Mar 2002 run with Larsen A/B in the mask. Both are driven by ERA-Interim, reinitialized every 12 h, with the 12 h spin-up discarded.
steps.quote: The model is reinitialized every 12 hr and runs for 24 hr.

steps.action: Authors build two foehn-detection algorithms. One is isentrope-based (after King et al. 2017) for station grid points; the other is an adapted Turton et al. (2018) humidity/temperature method for spatial maps.
steps.quote: an isentrope-based method adapted from the broad-scale approach of King et al. (2017) is adopted

steps.action: Authors check in the supplement (Section S2) that the two foehn-identification methods give comparable results.
steps.quote: showed that the two methods of identifying foehn events produced comparable results

steps.action: Authors compare modelled near-surface meteorology and SEB against AWS observations (Table 1, Figure 2, supplementary Tables S3-S4 for seasons and foehn/nonfoehn). They find warm, windy, moist biases and Emelt underestimated by 17-31%, most during foehn.
steps.quote: This makes the MetUM hindcast on average slightly warmer, windier, and moister than observations

steps.action: Authors attribute the biases to auxiliaries rather than rejecting the hindcast: boundary-layer mixing, the ERA-Interim warm bias, orography and the zero-layer snow scheme.
steps.quote: The warm bias in air and surface temperatures is likely to be at least partially related to the representation of boundary-layer

steps.action: Authors compare seasonal SEB means and diurnal cycles over Larsen C with ERA5 (Table 2, Figures S2-S3). They find broad agreement and differences attributed to resolution and foehn representation.
steps.quote: We additionally compare the hindcast against ERA5 reanalysis.

steps.action: Authors produce 19 melt-year maps and statistics of cumulative meltwater over Larsen C (Figures 3-4). Ice-shelf means range from 86 to 188 mm w.e. per year, with inlet maxima up to 1,025 mm w.e.
steps.quote: cumulative annual simulated meltwater production for all full melt years included in the hindcast period

steps.action: Authors check the melt patterns against independent estimates. Satellite melt-day observations (Bevan 2018, Luckman 2014) match, though two melt years are missed. Satellite/model magnitudes (Trusel 2013, 2015) suggest an ice-shelf-mean underestimate.
steps.quote: is consistent with satellite observations of the annual number of days that surface melting occurs

steps.action: Authors attribute the melt underestimate to the zero-layer snow model, the diagnostic albedo and under-captured foehn intensity.
steps.quote: Part of this may be explained by the simple zero-layer snow model and diagnostic albedo implementation.

steps.action: Authors select the past event before the Larsen B collapse (Sept 2001-Feb 2002) as a case study, using the run with Larsen B intact.
steps.quote: we now consider as a case study the period immediately preceding the collapse of Larsen B

steps.action: Authors estimate cumulative melt over Larsen B (mean 340, peak 664 mm w.e.) and the driving conditions (Figures 5-6). These are strong westerly flow, large turbulent fluxes in the lee of the mountains, and a mean Etot of 32 W m-2.
steps.quote: Mean cumulative surface melt of 340 mm w.e. is modeled across the Larsen B ice shelf

steps.action: Authors compare the Larsen B melt magnitude and drivers with published observations: Trusel 2015 (~725 mm w.e.), van den Broeke 2005 and Cape et al. 2015.
steps.quote: This magnitude of melt is comparable

steps.action: Authors estimate foehn frequency for 1998-2017 at stations (Table 3) and across the shelf (Figure 7). Seasonal means and standard deviations are given, with a gradient declining away from the mountains.
steps.quote: foehn events occurring on average 16% of the time annually at inlet stations and 13% of the time at ice shelf stations

steps.action: Authors compare the modelled foehn frequencies with values from previous AWS, model and satellite studies (6-20%).
steps.quote: comparable values to those cited in the aforementioned studies

steps.action: Authors infer from the qualitative similarity of the foehn and melt gradients that foehn plays a key role in melt. The test is deferred to Part 2.
steps.quote: suggesting a key role for foehn in causing surface melt

steps.action: Authors select the high-foehn, high-melt period of MAM 2016 as a second case study, placed in the 20-year hindcast context.
steps.quote: Unusually frequent and intense foehn flow was simulated in the hindcast during the second half of MAM 2016

steps.action: Authors estimate meteorological and SEB anomalies for 15 Apr-31 May 2016 against the model climatology (Figures 8-9, Table 4). Results include large HS anomalies and 5.7 Gt of melt (35.4% of the 2015/16 melt year), with melt streams in foehn jet regions.
steps.quote: Strong cross-peninsula flow is simulated

steps.action: Authors compare the MAM 2016 anomalies, foehn occurrence and melt fraction with Kuipers Munneke et al. 2018, Datta et al. 2019 and Wiesenekker et al. 2018, and the jet locations with Elvidge et al. 2015.
steps.quote: These modeled anomalies agree well with the observational and model data

steps.action: Authors keep the claim that the hindcast is a novel, adequately validated data set and tool for studying Larsen C melt. They acknowledge the snow and albedo limitations.
steps.quote: The high-resolution regional model hindcast presented here is a novel data set

tree.answer: Foehn-driven surface melt with an east-west gradient on Larsen C, already established in the literature
Only sparsely (four AWSs, satellite melt days); shelf-wide melt and SEB fields must be modelled
Build and validate a multidecadal high-resolution hindcast as a tool
No rival hypotheses; contrast only with hydrostatic or coarse models
Conditions found: past case studies (Larsen B 2001/02, MAM 2016) rerun in the model

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: 19 melt years and many foehn events give repeated cases for climatology
Partly: patterns and timing survive comparisons with AWS, ERA5, satellite and published values; melt magnitude underestimated
Hindcast judged a useful tool (capability characterized)

end.claim: The 4 km MetUM hindcast reproduces observed near-surface meteorology, the foehn-related east-west melt gradient and interannual melt variability on Larsen C, and is a useful tool for exploring the causes of surface melt.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the nonhydrostatic 4 km MetUM configuration able to resolve foehn flow over the Peninsula, there would be no multidecadal hindcast whose validation is the claim.

gates.evidence: Action: the expectation that a nonhydrostatic 4 km model resolves foehn directed the model configuration (p. 2, 4), but no hypothesis directed observational data acquisition. Claim: the hindcast was compared against AWS, ERA5, satellite and published values and could have failed (p. 6-14). However, no acceptance thresholds were stated, and mismatches (melt underestimated by 17-31%, missed melt years) were absorbed into 'reasonable accuracy'. Registration: nothing was reported as fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: semi-implicit semi-Lagrangian discretization (ENDGAME dynamical core) on an Arakawa-C grid
linear least squares regression and correlation coefficients for model-observation scatterplots

novelty_claims.quote: a new, high-resolution (4 km grid spacing) Met Office Unified Model (MetUM) hindcast of atmospheric conditions and surface melt processes
In contrast with previous model simulations, the MetUM captures the observed east-west gradient in surface melting associated with foehn winds
It represents an improvement on previous studies
The high-resolution regional model hindcast presented here is a novel data set

limits: The supplement (Sections S1-S2, Tables S3-S4, Figures S1-S5) was not supplied, so the foehn-method sensitivity test and the seasonal validation are coded from main-text descriptions only. No acceptance criteria for 'reasonable accuracy' are stated. Comparison with satellite melt patterns is by visual inspection (p. 14), and some comparisons rest on published values rather than reanalysis of the data. The AWS data are coded 'cited' because they were provided by another group (Acknowledgments); who applied the temperature and tilt corrections is not explicit (inference). No review file was supplied, though the acknowledgments mention reviewers, so no review sequence is coded. The foehn-melt causal link is only suggested here and deferred to Part 2 (sub-claim at status none here). The case-study sub-claims are at estimate level without stated uncertainties: Larsen B melt magnitude and drivers, and MAM 2016 anomalies (inference: closest to estimate_with_resolution, but no resolution is given). Step 5 (inherited) is kept separate from step 4 despite sharing node and mode because the move differs. The choice of the 4 km model over alternatives was not tested here but inherited from the authors' thesis.

disagreements.target: Datta et al. (2018, 2019) MAR simulations and van Wessem et al. (2015, 2016) RACMO simulations
disagreements.support: The paper argues that hydrostatic, coarse-resolution models underrepresent foehn dynamics, and shows that its nonhydrostatic 4 km hindcast reproduces the east-west melt gradient seen in satellite data.
disagreements.quote: resulting in a much weaker east-west gradient in climatological melting than observed

disagreements.target: MAR and RACMO models (community regional climate models)
disagreements.support: Concedes these models have better snow and albedo schemes but argues they simulate foehn less well because they are hydrostatic and coarser.
disagreements.quote: MAR and RACMO are hydrostatic and so simulate foehn flows less well

disagreements.target: Elvidge et al. (2015), who argued that about 1.5 km grid spacing is needed to resolve foehn over Larsen C
disagreements.support: Cites improvements in the ENDGAME dynamical core (Wood et al. 2014) and the lead author's thesis to argue that 4 km now suffices.
disagreements.quote: this argument was based on the previous version of the dynamical core

disagreements.target: Kuipers Munneke et al. (2018) on intense winter melt in 2016
disagreements.support: Uses 20 years of hindcast to show that MAM 2016 foehn and melt were far above the model climatology, putting the 2-year observational result in context.
disagreements.quote: Only 2 years of observations were used in the Kuipers Munneke et al. study, which made it difficult to determine how anomalous these conditions were.

alternatives_considered.alternatives: about 1.5 km grid spacing (Elvidge et al. 2015)
alternatives_considered.reason: ENDGAME improvements give a more accurate flow response to orography, so about 4 km is now sufficient (Gilbert 2020)

alternatives_considered.chosen: RA1M configuration with modified large-scale cloud and precipitation parameterization
alternatives_considered.alternatives: other model configurations, evaluated in Gilbert et al. (2020)
alternatives_considered.reason: Gilbert et al. (2020) showed it was the most suitable configuration available for the region

alternatives_considered.chosen: isentrope-based foehn method at station grid points and adapted Turton et al. (2018) method for spatial maps
alternatives_considered.reason: the isentrope method is too computationally expensive for every grid point

alternatives_considered.chosen: Turton et al. conditions (a) and (c) plus a westerly-wind stipulation
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Turton et al. condition (b), a location-specific RH threshold

alternatives_considered.chosen: land-sea mask without Larsen A and B for the main hindcast; modified mask with Larsen A and B for the 2001/02 run
alternatives_considered.alternatives: a single mask for both runs
alternatives_considered.reason: the case study focuses on conditions over Larsen B before its collapse

alternatives_considered.chosen: grouping stations into 'ice shelf' (AWS 14/15) and 'inlet' (AWS 17/18) means, and showing only AWS 14 scatterplots
alternatives_considered.reason: time series similar enough to justify grouping; AWS 14 has the longest record and results are broadly similar

alternatives_considered.chosen: zero-layer snow scheme with diagnostic albedo
alternatives_considered.alternatives: multilayer JULES snow model and prognostic albedo
alternatives_considered.reason: none given; acknowledged as a limitation and future priority
